research.approach: Practitioners start by fixing the returns data: a reason on every return, logged by product and size, with fit kept apart from quality and expectation. They benchmark the rate by category and product, then read the fit pattern (too small versus too large, one size, one product, several sizes in one order) because each pattern needs a different fix. They put the cost on each reason so effort goes where money is lost, fix the worst products first with product-specific fit notes and measured garment sizes rather than a generic chart, and measure by changing a set of products while comparable ones stay as a control, across a full sell-through. Policy responses to bracketing come last.

steps.name: Get a usable reason on every return
steps.why: With 60% of reasons blank, no cause can be named. Practitioners turn on specific, apparel-aware reason choices and log the product and size.

steps.name: Pull returns and orders and benchmark by product, size and customer
steps.why: A 31% average hides which products and sizes drive it, and what is normal for this category.

steps.name: Check the returns data before reasoning from it
steps.why: Blank reasons, the definition of the rate and exchanges counted as returns all change the answer.

steps.name: Read the pattern and separate fit from quality and expectation
steps.why: Too small and too big in equal numbers means weak guidance, one direction means a wrong size run, one size means production, several sizes in an order means bracketing.

steps.name: Put a rupee cost on each reason and product
steps.why: Effort should follow money lost: refunds, Rs 180 return shipping and stock that cannot be resold.

steps.name: Fix the worst products first with measured, product-specific fit information
steps.why: A generic size chart helps little. Measured garment sizes, fit notes and size-up or size-down prompts on the flagged products address the usual cause.

steps.name: Respond to bracketing and serial returners with policy
steps.why: Practitioners push exchanges over refunds and add restocking terms, but these change the returns policy.

steps.name: Change a set of products and compare with unchanged ones over a full sell-through
steps.why: Returns arrive weeks after the order. A control group of similar products shows what the changes did.

pitfalls.text: Assuming sizing is the cause from the 40% of returns that gave a reason, when the blank 60% may differ.
Fixing one generic size chart for the whole store instead of the few products that drive returns.
Counting bracketing (several sizes bought, one kept) as a size chart problem.
Reading results before returns from the changed orders have come in.
Treating vendor percentages for fit returns as this store's numbers.

hypotheses.statement: Published size charts do not match the garments, so shoppers pick the wrong size.
hypotheses.test: Compare measured garment sizes with the published chart for the top-returning products; read fit comments in reviews.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The chart differs from measured garments by a size or more on those products, or reviews often say it runs small or large.
hypotheses.refute_if: Charts match measurements and reviews do not mention fit.

hypotheses.statement: A small number of products or sizes cause most returns.
hypotheses.test: Return rate and share of all returns by product and size, with a minimum number of orders.
hypotheses.confirm_if: A few products or sizes have a return rate far above the store average and make up a large share of returns.
hypotheses.refute_if: Returns are spread evenly across products and sizes.

hypotheses.statement: Shoppers buy two or more sizes of one style and return the extras.
hypotheses.test: Orders with the same style in several sizes, and what share of their lines are returned.
hypotheses.confirm_if: A large share of returned lines come from multi-size orders of one style.
hypotheses.refute_if: Returned lines mostly come from single-size orders.

hypotheses.statement: Items are returned because colour, fabric or look differs from the page.
hypotheses.test: Reviews and any reason notes that mention colour, material, see-through or not as pictured, by product.
hypotheses.confirm_if: These themes are frequent on the products with the highest return rates.
hypotheses.refute_if: They are rare compared with fit comments.

hypotheses.statement: A quality or defect problem on certain batches drives returns.
hypotheses.test: Return reasons and review themes for damage, stitching, shrinkage or defects by product and order date.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Defect themes cluster on specific products or supplier batches.
hypotheses.refute_if: Defect themes are rare and spread out.

hypotheses.statement: The 60% of returns with no reason differ from the 40% that have one, so the sizing theory may rest on a biased sample.
hypotheses.test: Compare product, size, order value and review themes for blank versus reasoned returns.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Blank-reason returns are concentrated in different products or customers than reasoned ones.
hypotheses.refute_if: The two groups look alike on product, size and value.

hypotheses.statement: A small group of customers returns a large share of items.
hypotheses.test: Returns per customer over the period, and the share of returned lines from the top 5% of returners.
hypotheses.confirm_if: A small group accounts for a large share of returns.
hypotheses.refute_if: Returns are spread across many customers.

measurement.window: Orders placed in the 4 weeks after each change, read once the return window for those orders has passed, compared with control products over the same weeks.
measurement.min_volume: At least 100 orders per group (changed and control), or the result is INCONCLUSIVE.
measurement.stop_rule: Roll a change back early only if order volume on the changed products drops sharply or return shipping cost per return rises; otherwise read the full window.
